title: Can you prepare for case interviews without a business background?
description: Encouragement and a practical plan for engineers, scientists, doctors, lawyers and anyone new to business who is preparing for case interviews.
hook: Yes. Case interviews test how you reason, not what you know about business, and the core skills (breaking a problem down, forming and testing a hypothesis, working with numbers and explaining your conclusion) are ones engineers, scientists, doctors and lawyers already use. What you need to add is a working business vocabulary, a few standard ways of structuring problems, and plenty of practice talking through cases out loud. This guide shows what transfers, what to learn, and how to plan your preparation.
body:
In this guide

  • Why a business degree is not the point
  • What you already have
  • What to add
  • A worked example: the café with falling profit
  • Turn your background into an advantage
  • Explaining your move in the fit interview
  • Mistakes non-business candidates make
  • A realistic plan
  • Check yourself

Why a business degree is not the point

A case interview is not an exam on business facts. The interviewer gives you the information that matters (the market size, the costs, the competitor's price) and watches what you do with it. The firms say there is no single right answer; what they score is your approach. That puts you on much more even ground than it might seem.

The real gap for most non-business candidates is narrower than they fear: some vocabulary, a feel for how companies make money, and practice at thinking out loud. All three are learnable in a few weeks.

What you already have

BackgroundSkill you already useWhere it shows up in a case
ScienceForm a hypothesis, isolate variables, revise on evidenceStating a hypothesis early and testing it with data
EngineeringBreak a system into components, find the bottleneckIssue trees, operations and capacity cases
MedicineDiagnose from symptoms, rule causes in or out, decide under uncertaintyProfitability and "why has this fallen?" cases
LawBuild an argument, weigh evidence, anticipate objectionsStructuring, recommendations and handling pushback
Teaching or researchExplain complex ideas simply to a live audienceCommunication throughout, and the final recommendation

Comfort with numbers matters too. Case maths is simpler than most technical maths: percentages, growth rates, margins and multiplication. The challenge is doing it out loud and quickly, not the maths itself.

What to add

Business vocabulary

Start with the consulting glossary and how businesses make money. You need to be comfortable with about thirty terms: revenue, fixed and variable costs, margin, contribution margin, break-even, market share, churn, capex, payback and a handful more. Learn them with an example each, not as definitions.

A few standard structures

Not to memorise, but to recognise the usual shapes: profit = revenue − costs; revenue = volume × price; "should we enter this market?" breaks into the market, the competition, our ability to win and the economics. Which framework to use covers the eleven that handle most cases.

Commercial instinct

Ten minutes a day reading business news and asking two questions, "How does this company make money?" and "What would I do in their position?", builds judgement faster than you would expect. Building business judgement gives you a routine.

A worked example: the café with falling profit

You do not need an MBA to make progress on a classic case. Take this prompt: "A small café's profit has fallen. Why?"

  1. Start with the definition. Profit = revenue − costs. Ask which has changed. Say revenue has fallen and costs are flat.
  2. Split revenue. Revenue = number of transactions × average spend per transaction.
  3. Use the numbers. Last year: 60,000 transactions × $8.00 = $480k. This year: 54,000 × $8.50 = $459k. Revenue is down $21k.
  4. Find the driver. Transactions fell 10% (6,000 ÷ 60,000). Average spend rose about 6% ($0.50 ÷ $8.00). So the problem is fewer customers, partly hidden by each one spending more. Had spend stayed at $8.00, revenue would have fallen to $432k.
  5. Ask why. Is footfall down (a new competitor, roadworks, an office closing nearby) or are fewer passers-by coming in? Did a recent price rise push some regulars away?
  6. Avoid the obvious trap. Proposing a price increase would make things worse if price is what drove customers away.

That is exactly how a doctor works through symptoms: define the problem, split it into parts, find which part has changed, then look for the cause. The business words are new; the reasoning is not.

Turn your background into an advantage

Interviewers enjoy candidates who bring real experience. A doctor who mentions how a hospital bed gets blocked by a delayed discharge, or an engineer who knows how one slow machine limits a whole production line, sounds more credible than a candidate reciting a framework.

Use what you know briefly and only when it helps the case. One sentence such as "In hospitals, the bottleneck is often discharge rather than admissions, so I'd check that first" shows insight. Five minutes on hospital procedure loses the thread.

Explaining your move in the fit interview

Expect "Why consulting?" and expect follow-ups about why you are leaving your field. Answer in a way that respects your past rather than escaping it.

Weak: "I'm leaving medicine because the hours are bad and I want to be in business."
Strong: "I loved diagnosing problems for one patient at a time. Running a quality project on our ward showed me I enjoy fixing problems that affect a whole system, and consulting lets me do that across many organisations."

The strong version links a real experience to what consultants do. Strong and weak "Why consulting?" answers has more examples.

Mistakes non-business candidates make

  • Borrowing jargon you cannot explain. Saying "synergies" or "value chain" without being able to define them invites a follow-up you cannot answer. Plain words are fine. When you meet a term you do not know in a case, ask what it means.
  • Being too precise. Scientists and engineers often calculate to three decimal places. Cases reward sensible rounding: 54,000 × $8.50 is "about $460k", and that is enough to decide.
  • Answering like an academic. Context, method, caveats and then the conclusion is the wrong order. Give the answer first, then the reasons.
  • Hiding your background. Trying to sound like a business graduate wastes your strongest asset.
  • Waiting until you "know enough" to practise. Start full cases in week two, not week five.

A realistic plan

Give yourself more time than a business student would, ideally six weeks. Use the six-week plan and spend a little longer in the first phase: two weeks on the course, the glossary and how businesses make money, with easy cases from the start. Then move quickly into four or five full cases a week.

Three exercises are especially useful for you:

  • Explain the economics of a business you use every day in one minute: who pays, for what, and what it costs to serve them.
  • Turn a news story into a testable hypothesis: "If this airline is cutting routes, I'd expect its utilisation is low on them."
  • Deliver a 30-second recommendation that includes one number.

Check yourself

1. In the café case, what if transactions had stayed at 60,000 and spend had fallen to $7.65?

Show the answer

Revenue would be 60,000 × $7.65 = $459k, the same fall of $21k. But now the problem is spend per customer, so you would look at the menu mix, discounting and whether customers are skipping the food and only buying coffee.

2. An interviewer asks you about "working capital" and you are not sure what they mean. What do you say?

Show the answer

Ask, briefly: "Just to make sure I'm answering the right question, do you mean the cash tied up in stock and unpaid customer invoices?" Asking is far better than guessing.

3. You are an engineer. Write one sentence that uses your background in an operations case about a slow warehouse.

Show the answer

Something like: "In production lines the slowest step sets the pace for everything, so I'd first find which stage, picking, packing or loading, has the longest queue." Short, relevant and testable.

Where to go next

Read what a case interview is, then start the course.
